title: The Lord in every heart
hook: ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai: the Lord dwells in every heart, as the holy proclaim (Salok M9, ang 1427)

segments.voice: Yesterday, none of it is yours, and your line: none of it goes. Did you add the word lent to one thing you called mine? If nothing we own goes along, what is it that's truly near? Today's salok answers. Day five hundred ninety-two.
screen: `NONE OF IT IS YOURS — NONE OF IT GOES.`

segments.voice: Sikh tradition tells of a man named Bhai Ghanaiya. During the battles around Anandpur, he carried a water skin across the battlefield and gave water to the wounded, to Sikhs and to the soldiers they were fighting. Some Sikhs were furious and brought him before Guru Gobind Singh. The Guru asked him why he was helping the enemy. And Bhai Ghanaiya is remembered as answering that he saw no enemy. In every face, he said, he saw only the Guru. The Guru, the story says, gave him ointment as well, and told him to bandage their wounds too.
screen: `BHAI GHANAIYA'S WATER SKIN.` → `WATER FOR BOTH SIDES.` → `IN EVERY FACE, THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Bhai Ghanaiya's answer echoes today's salok, written by Guru Gobind Singh's own father. Ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai, santan kahio pukaar. In paraphrase: the Lord dwells in every heart; the holy ones have proclaimed it aloud. Then: says Nanak, meditate on Him, O mind, and you'll cross the terrifying ocean. Ghatt is a lovely word. It means a clay pot, a vessel, and from that, the body or heart that holds a life. Ghatt ghatt: pot after pot, every single vessel. Not just the devout ones, or the kind ones, or our own people. Every vessel. And pukaar means a loud call, a shout. The salok says the holy haven't whispered this. They've called it out. Last week, in the forest hymn, the Lord was within like scent in a flower: that was about finding God inside yourself. This salok turns the same teaching outward. Every vessel means mine, and yours. And the stranger's. And the soldier's on the other side. That's what makes it hard. Seeing God in the people we love comes more easily. The salok doesn't stop there. Sikhs see the same line at work in langar, which feeds anyone who walks in, of any faith or none, seated together on the floor. Seva, service, isn't reserved for members either. In every heart means every heart. And Bhai Ghanaiya's water skin is what that line looks like when someone lives it.
screen: `GHATT GHATT: EVERY VESSEL.` · `PUKAAR: THE HOLY CALL IT ALOUD.` · `TURNED OUTWARD: THE STRANGER TOO.` · `LANGAR FEEDS ANYONE.` · then, large: `IN EVERY HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see Him in one heart. Bring to mind one person you find difficult. Not your worst enemy, just someone who annoys you, or someone you've written off. Picture their face. Now picture the salok's clay vessel, and remember what it says lives inside every one. You don't have to like them. Just let the thought sit: the Lord dwells here too. Notice what softens, and what resists. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru for one breath. The bell holds the time.
The Lord in every heart. Ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai: the salok says the Lord lives in every vessel, every heart, as the holy proclaim aloud.
screen: `THE LORD IN EVERY HEART — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in every heart. Today, do one small kindness for someone you'd normally pass by, or someone on the other side of an argument. Day five hundred ninety-two.

screen: `DAY 592 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: UNTOUCHED BY PAIN AND PLEASURE.`

howItsDone: Sikhs serve langar to anyone who comes, seated together on the floor, and remember Bhai Ghanaiya, who gave water to the wounded on both sides, as a model of seeing the Lord in every heart.

fork.setup: you're Guru Gobind Singh. a Sikh is brought before you for giving water to the enemy's wounded. what do you do?
options: punish him for helping the enemy.
ask why, then give him ointment for their wounds too.
fork.reveal: tradition says Bhai Ghanaiya answered that he saw only the Guru in every face, and the Guru gave him ointment to bandage their wounds as well.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ghatt, a clay pot, a vessel, and so the body or heart. Ghatt ghatt: in every one.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Lord in every heart is a nice thought about inner peace.
what it means: it turns outward: the same Lord lives in the stranger and the opponent, so they are owed care too.
what a scholar hears: ghatt, a clay water pot, is an old Indian image for the body as a vessel holding a life, and Gurbani uses it constantly for the heart where the Lord is found.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 12 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): narrator no longer states belief as fact ('this truth', 'if the Lord lives in my heart, He lives in yours', 'the same light that's in you'); 'almost a quotation' softened to 'echoes'; 'across the centuries' and the causal claim about langar softened; 'twelfth' dropped from the spoken word line (numbering left for the Keeper).
Paraphrase of salok 12 (ghat ghat mai har joo basai santan kahio pukaar; kaho naanak tih bhaj manaa bhau nidh utrahi paar): please confirm wording, numbering and Ang 1427.
Bhai Ghanaiya story told as tradition; details (ointment, 'I saw only the Guru') follow the common telling.
